newsitem.title: INDONESIA: ACPC should show it's not coffee cartel - Indonesia.
newsitem.headline: ACPC should show it's not coffee cartel - Indonesia.

text.p: It is timely for the Association of Coffee Producing Countries (ACPC) to demonstrate to consumers it is not a cartel, an Indonesian official said on Friday, a day after coffee prices surged to 20-year highs.
"We should demonstrate that we are not a cartel by taking into account the interest of consumers," Paian Nainggolan, Indonesia's representative to the ACPC, told Reuters.
"The day we launched the ACPC, we made it clear it will not be a cartel," he said ahead of the technical committee and full council meetings of the ACPC next week in London.
Nainggolan declined to say how the 14-member grouping could demonstrate it cared for consumers who have had to pay more for their brew following a steady hike in prices.

Coffee prices soared to 20-year highs on Thursday in New York in an explosive rally on frantic buying from speculators and commercial coffee firms worried about small coffee stockpiles and shrinking crop prospects.
Coffee for May delivery closed at 277.05 cents a pound, up 15.55 cents, after trading as high as 279.00 cents -- the highest price for a coffee futures contract since June 1977.
In London, the benchmark July contract jumped $70 to a new year-high of $1,940 a tonne before closing at $1,933 a tonne.
Nainggolan said Indonesia would make no specific proposal at the ACPC meeting, adding that "there were no proposals on the table" for the technical committee meeting on May 19.
"We will attend the meeting with an open mind," he said.
Industry sources said on Thursday the ACPC council meeting on May 21 might delay taking a decision over fresh export quotas in view of significant gains in coffee prices.
The ACPC is to review its 12-month export programme which expires at the end of June at its council meeting.
The programme is aimed at capping members' exports at 25.48 million bags in the first half of 1997 through a quota system.
In January, the member countries cut exports by 1.3 million bags but at a subsequent meeting in March, they decided to put back some 500,000 bags back into the market.

Indonesia, the world's third largest producer after Brazil and Colombia, was allocated an export quota of 6.0 million bags under the 1996/97 (July-June) export programme, up from 4.6 million bags in 1995/96.
